Juvenile Blacklip abalone typically recruit to subtidal reefs after a brief planktonic larval phase, settling preferentially on crustose coralline algae. Upon metamorphosis, the newly settled spat measure only a few hundred microns in shell length, and the wet weight of a newly hatched larva is remarkably small. Data on early life stages indicate that the wet weight at birth is 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], a value that underscores the minuscule size of the fertilized egg, which has a diameter of approximately 0.02 mm. As the juveniles grow, they begin grazing on biofilm and drift algae, and their shell width expands steadily. In females, the onset of reproductive capability is attained at a shell width of 9.7 cm [Lp = 9.7 cm], a measurement that marks the transition to the adult phase. This size threshold is consistent with observations from wild populations across the species' range, where shell width at puberty for females typically falls between 3 and 9 cm. Reaching this dimension usually requires several years of sustained growth, as individuals allocate resources to somatic development before shifting energy toward gamete production.

Under stable thermal conditions typical of their cool-temperate habitat, Blacklip abalone exhibit a relatively long lifespan. When reared at a constant water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum longevity recorded for this species is approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of many haliotid gastropods and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes slow, steady growth and repeated reproductive events over many seasons. In the wild, individuals may not always achieve this maximum potential due to predation, disease, or environmental stressors, but the physiological capacity for such longevity is well documented from tag-recapture studies and captive maintenance records. The ability to survive for two decades allows multiple spawning seasons, contributing to population resilience.

Adult Blacklip abalone can attain a considerable ultimate shell width, with maximum recorded values reaching 20 cm [Li = 20 cm]. Individuals approaching this size are typically older specimens that have experienced favorable conditions, including abundant food resources and minimal disturbance. The shell shape is broadly oval and the exterior surface is often encrusted with epibionts, reflecting a long period of exposure on the open reef. Comparative studies with congeneric species such as Haliotis tuberculata suggest that the relationship between shell length and body mass is broadly similar across the genus. For Haliotis rubra, the shell-free wet weight of a large adult is estimated from allometric equations to be approximately 433.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 433.3 grams], a value derived from data on related abalone species. This substantial soft-tissue mass supports a large gonad that can produce millions of gametes during a single spawning season, enabling high fecundity.

Reproduction in Blacklip abalone is characterized by high fecundity and a pronounced spawning season. The maximum reproduction rate, when measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], corresponds to a daily egg output of approximately 20,547 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 20,547 eggs per day]. This value is calculated from the annual reproductive output, which can reach 7.5 million eggs per female per year. The high fecundity is an adaptation to the pelagic larval phase, during which mortality rates are extremely high; only a tiny fraction of the larvae successfully settle and metamorphose into juveniles. Spawning events are typically synchronized with seasonal temperature cues, and a single female may release multiple batches of eggs over the course of the reproductive period. The energetic cost of producing such a large number of oocytes is substantial, but is offset by the abundant food resources available in kelp-dominated habitats.

Ecologically, Blacklip abalone play a key role as grazers in temperate reef communities, controlling the abundance of macroalgae and maintaining bare space for encrusting organisms. Their slow growth and late maturity, combined with high fecundity and the capacity to live for approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] under optimal conditions, place them at the slow end of the life-history continuum among marine gastropods at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The species is also of considerable commercial importance, supporting both a wild fishery and an aquaculture industry. Management strategies often rely on size limits, with the 9.7 cm [Lp = 9.7 cm] threshold for female puberty serving as a key reference point for minimum legal sizes in some jurisdictions. The relatively slow somatic growth means that recovery from overfishing can take many years, and the maximum longevity provides a buffer against short-term fluctuations in recruitment. Conservation efforts focus on maintaining adequate broodstock densities to ensure consistent larval supply.
